title: Pray for one another (James 5:13–20)
hook: sick? call the elders; suffering? pray; cheerful? sing

segments.voice: Yesterday: the patient farmer, and Job, whose patience argued and still held on. Your line was be patient.

Some letters end with a long goodbye. James doesn't. No greetings, no names, no farewell. His last paragraph reads like a list on the fridge before a long trip: if this happens, do this. Sad? Happy? Sick? Wandering? There's an instruction for each. And almost every one points to the same thing. Not a technique, not a rule. Other people, and prayer. The last word of a blunt, practical letter is about how a community holds each other up.

In the King James Bible: "Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms." Every mood has a place to go: hard days, bring them to God; good days, sing. Then: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice who moves. The sick person calls, and the elders come to the bedside. Oil was a common medicine in the ancient world, and also a sign of being set apart for God. Churches practice this verse differently. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, it's one of the roots of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick. Many Protestant churches also anoint and pray over the sick, as a practice of prayer rather than a sacrament. Then: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." One to another: not only up to God, but sideways, to each other. And James's example is encouraging. Elijah, he says, was a man subject to like passions as we are. An ordinary human, moody, tired, frightened at times. He prayed, and rain was held back; he prayed again, and it came. You don't need to be a giant; ordinary people's prayers matter. The very last line: whoever brings back someone who has wandered from the truth saves a soul and covers a multitude of sins. The letter ends not with a farewell, but with someone going after someone else.

Think of someone who is ill right now, a friend, a parent, a child, someone you've only heard about, and picture where they are and what they might be feeling. If you pray, pray for them by name in your own words, one for another, as James says; if you don't, hold them in your attention with care and wish them well.
Elders. The ones the sick are told to call in James's last instructions: come to the bedside, pray, anoint with oil, and hold each other up.
Your line: going after someone who wandered. That's where James chooses to end his letter. Six hundred eighty days, and counting.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians celebrate the anointing of the sick as a sacrament based in part on James 5:14–15, and many Protestant churches have elders or ministers anoint and pray over the sick; most churches also pray for the sick by name in worship.

chat.says: When someone in the church is sick, what does James actually say to do?
options: Call the elders to come pray over them and anoint them with oil, and pray for one another.
Wait until they're better, then have them come back and sing psalms with everyone.
Only pray if you're as holy as Elijah; ordinary people's prayers don't carry much.
chat.meaning: James says the sick should call the elders, who come to pray and anoint with oil, and that believers pray one for another.

elders.meaning: church leaders the sick are told to call

anointing.meaning: putting oil on someone as a sign, with prayer

sacrament.meaning: a sacred rite; for Catholics and Orthodox, the anointing of the sick

Elijah.meaning: a prophet whose prayers held back the rain, then brought it

psalms.meaning: songs and prayers from the Bible's book of Psalms

notes: Anointing of the sick: Catholic and Orthodox sacrament (Holy Unction in Orthodox usage); Protestant practice varies. Confirm fair description.
Oil as medicine in the ancient world (cf. Luke 10:34): standard background; confirm.
πρεσβύτερος and English 'priest' (via Latin presbyter): standard etymology.
Elijah's drought and rain: 1 Kings 17–18; James 5:17 gives three years and six months.
Practice adapted ('pray for one sick person, or hold them in mind') so anyone can do it.
